profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a university research computing center about the first rollout of a lightweight requirements-engineering workflow for a shared epidemiological simulation platform used by multiple research groups. The team is responding to recurring confusion about feature requests, undocumented assumptions, and last-minute model changes, and wants to pilot a more structured approach inspired by recent work on requirements engineering for research software. The agenda is to decide what the pilot includes, which research team will use it first, how requirements will be captured during existing collaborations, who owns each setup task, and what 'ready' means for the target date before the center's quarterly methods review. The expected outcome is a concrete implementation plan for the pilot, including scope, pilot users, responsibilities, and timeline.

members.name: Nina Alvarez
members.expertise: Stakeholder discovery, workflow design, cross-team delivery in academic software environments
members.background: Nina previously worked as a product lead for a nonprofit data platform and now coordinates feature planning across several university research software projects, translating scientist requests into development plans.
members.private_state: She wants a visibly successful pilot before the quarterly methods review, with minimal disruption to researchers and a deliverable she can present as a repeatable process for other labs.
hidden_assumptions: A 'requirements template' should be lightweight enough that researchers can complete it inside existing meetings, so it mainly means a short intake form plus a place to capture open questions.
If something is 'ready for the pilot,' it is usable by one real team in staging with example entries and a short walkthrough, even if training materials and process refinements are still rough.
When people mention 'the transmission model team,' they usually mean the influenza forecasting collaborators because they are the most active external requesters this semester.
Requirements capture during weekly research syncs works best if engineers listen to discussion and summarize afterward, because researchers rarely pre-fill structured documents.
A pilot scope should avoid adding governance-style artifacts like decision rationale logs unless they are necessary to unblock adoption.

members.name: Dr. Samir Patel
members.expertise: Scientific workflow tooling, reproducibility, model lifecycle support, software process for computational science
members.background: Samir has spent eight years building simulation and data-analysis systems for public health and climate projects, and is known for introducing process improvements that preserve traceability for publications and grant audits.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to demonstrate that structured requirements can improve reproducibility, not just intake efficiency, and he worries that an overly thin rollout will create another abandoned process.
hidden_assumptions: A 'requirements template' needs enough structure to preserve rationale and downstream impact, which means intake fields plus decision history and change tracking from the start.
If something is 'ready for the pilot,' the process is stable enough that researchers can follow it without hand-holding, including written guidance and clearly assigned ownership.
When people refer to 'the transmission model team,' they mean the COVID mobility project because that group has the messiest evolving assumptions and is the real stress test.
Capturing requirements in weekly research syncs means principal investigators or analysts enter requests before the meeting so the discussion can refine them rather than reconstruct them afterward.
For research software, omitting rationale early creates rework later because publication-driven changes are hard to interpret without a trace of why decisions were made.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the requirements template
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'set up the requirements template' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a lightweight intake template: request summary, affected workflow, urgency, and open questions, likely one page in the team workspace.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a fuller structured template: intake fields plus rationale, assumptions, dependencies, and a change-history section suitable for scientific traceability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as advocating a practical template rather than debating scope, and 'requirements template' sounds like a settled artifact whose exact fields can be filled in later, so neither expects a hidden semantic gap.

misalignment_points.topic: What team is the pilot user
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that they should pilot with 'the transmission model team.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the influenza forecasting collaborators who request frequent feature tweaks but are relatively easy to coordinate with.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the COVID mobility project, another transmission-model effort, whose requirements shift often and would better test process robustness.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams are informally described inside the organization as transmission-model work, and each participant assumes the other shares the locally obvious reference because no one expects ambiguity in the shorthand.

misalignment_points.topic: What ready for the pilot means
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree on getting the workflow 'ready for the pilot' before the quarterly methods review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the workflow is configured in staging, has one example project loaded, and can be demonstrated live with one research team next week.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the workflow has written guidance, ownership expectations, and enough process stability that researchers can actually use it without intensive facilitation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using the same milestone phrase in a planning context where readiness is normally taken as self-explanatory, and the review deadline pressures them toward discussing dates and owners rather than readiness criteria.

misalignment_points.topic: How requirements will be captured in weekly syncs
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'capture requirements during the weekly research sync.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes engineers or product staff will listen during the live sync, then summarize requests into the template afterward and send notes for confirmation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes researchers will enter initial requests before the sync, and the meeting will refine those entries and record rationale in real time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both methods are plausibly described as capturing requirements during the sync, and because the meeting is about planning the rollout rather than operational training, the exact workflow feels too mundane to spell out.

turns.inner_thought: I need something I can show at the quarterly methods review as a clean, repeatable pilot, and I can't afford to drag researchers into a heavy process redesign. If we can get one team using it in staging with an example and a short walkthrough, that's enough to call it ready for the pilot.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I'd like us to leave with today is a concrete plan for the first requirements workflow pilot on the epi platform, with enough in place that we're ready for the pilot before the quarterly methods review.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to prove more than that requests are easier to collect. We've had plenty of visible intake processes that died because they didn't help explain later changes. If the pilot doesn't improve traceability for scientific decisions, it won't stick.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'd just like the pilot to show that we're improving traceability around research software changes, not only making intake more visible.

turns.inner_thought: Best path is to keep the requirements template very lean: a short intake form in the existing workspace plus somewhere to note open questions. If it's lightweight, researchers won't resist it and I can get it stood up fast.
turns.utterance: Agreed. To get moving quickly, I think we should start by setting up the requirements template in the existing workspace so the first team can begin using it without a lot of change to their routine.

turns.inner_thought: The requirements template needs real structure from day one: not just the request, but assumptions, dependencies, rationale, and a change trail. Otherwise we'll recreate the same ambiguity we're trying to fix, and the pilot won't demonstrate reproducibility benefits.
turns.utterance: Yes, and as we set up the requirements template, I'd want to make sure it leaves room to capture assumptions and decision history so we can see why requests shift over time.

turns.inner_thought: The transmission model team is the influenza forecasting group in my mind. They're active, responsive, and manageable, which is exactly what I need for a visible first pass before the review.
turns.utterance: On pilot users, my vote would be to start with the transmission model team. They already send frequent requests, so we'd get feedback quickly and learn where the workflow needs adjustment.

turns.inner_thought: Good, the COVID mobility group is exactly the right stress test. Their assumptions move around constantly, and if the process works there, it'll work anywhere. Nina is landing in the same place I wanted.
turns.utterance: I agree, the transmission model team is the right place to pilot. The way their requests evolve should give the process a real stress test rather than an easy pass.

turns.inner_thought: I need a practical milestone, not a perfect one. If the workspace is configured in staging, there's one example loaded, and I can walk the team through it next week, then it's ready for the pilot from my perspective.
turns.utterance: From a timing standpoint, if the workspace is configured and we can walk one group through an example next week, I'd consider the workflow ready for the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: A demo is not enough. Ready for the pilot means researchers can follow it without me sitting beside them translating every field, and the ownership is clear enough that entries don't decay after week one.
turns.utterance: That works as a target, and when I think about being ready for the pilot, I also want the instructions clear enough that the researchers can follow the process consistently once they start.

turns.inner_thought: We should fit this into existing weekly syncs, not ask people to do prep work they won't do. Engineering can listen during the meeting, then summarize the discussion into the template afterward and circulate notes for confirmation.
turns.utterance: For the operating rhythm, I'd suggest we capture requirements during the weekly research sync. That keeps it inside a meeting they already attend and should make adoption easier.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I'll draft a format researchers can fill in before the sync so the meeting can refine it and record rationale while decisions are fresh. That's the only way 'capture requirements during the weekly research sync' will produce usable traceability.
turns.utterance: Yes, let's do that. I can draft a format for how we capture requirements during the weekly research sync so entries are in a good shape for discussion and refinement there.

turns.inner_thought: I'll handle the workspace and outreach to the influenza collaborators. Samir can prepare the requirements template and some light guidance. I don't want this to balloon into a governance package; just enough support to run the pilot and show it at the review.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll take the workspace setup and the outreach side, and Samir, if you're up for it, could you prepare the requirements template and the pilot guidance? That should give us a clean split and keep us on track.

turns.inner_thought: I'll build the fuller template and written guidance for the COVID mobility team, with enough structure that they can actually use it. If I can get that ready before the methods review, we have a chance to show this as a durable process, not another ad hoc intake form.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works. So we're setting up the requirements template, piloting with the transmission model team, capturing requirements during the weekly research sync, and aiming to have the workflow ready for the pilot ahead of the review. I'll have the materials prepared in time for that.
